Heat Recovery from Ventilation Systems NBC Subsection 9.36.8. requires an HRV as a prerequisite for compliance. This Article adds efficiency requirements for HRVs where they are installed. An HRV is not mandatory for compliance to Subsections other than NBC Subsection 9.36.8. There is a large variety of HRVs with a wide spectrum of efficiencies. This Article sets out the testing requirements with reference to the exterior temperature at the building location. The testing requirements cover a large number of HRVs already on the market. NBC Note A-9.36.3.9.(3) provides guidance on how to achieve compliance with NBC Sentence 9.36.3.9.(3) through HVI's Certified Home Ventilating Products Directory. 9.36.3.10. Equipment Efficiency This Article provides a table of the most common types of heating, cooling and ventilation equipment installed in housing and small buildings, along with the corresponding minimum efficiency values and performance standards for each. The authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) may

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: permit the use of equipment not included in this table, provided the specific performance and efficiency criteria are available and acceptable to the AHJ. The intent of this Article is to ensure that equipment used in the design, construction and operation of buildings is energy-efficient, that there is a consistent approach in the selection of equipment, and that, as much as possible, the NBC keeps pace with higher and more stringent energy efficiency standards and industry applications. The NECB is identified as an acceptable solution in NBC Section 9.36. Where the requirements of the NECB conflict with the requirements of the NBC, the requirements providing the greatest performance level govern. Federal, provincial and territorial energy efficiency Acts and regulations govern the type of equipment that can be traded across international, provincial and territorial borders. For equipment manufactured and sold within the same province or territory, the AHJ may confirm if other requirements apply. The energy efficiency ratings and performance requirements in NBC Table 9.36.3.10. are based on current regulations and standards for such domestic equipment. Minimum values set out in the energy efficiency Acts and regulations govern and were the values in these Acts and regulations to change in mid-Code cycle, those new values would take precedence. For combination and integrated mechanical systems that are supplied as one unit or package and where the system comprises multiple components, the efficiency of

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: the full unit should be based on each of the individual component efficiencies as provided by the specific component's manufacturer. For example, combination mechanical systems could include multiple components, such as space-heating equipment, service water heating equipment, and ventilation equipment. Natural gas and propane fireplaces or stoves are now included in the Article. The Notes: • include further detail on the use of decorative gas-fired fireplaces and stoves, • describe the use of and reference applicable standards for such appliances, and • provide clear instruction that such appliances may not be used to satisfy heating requirements within the building, as required by NBC Section 9.33. Decorative gas-fired fireplaces are those within the scope of ANSI Z21.50/CSA 2.22, “Vented decorative gas appliances,” and are marked as such on the rating plate. These appliances are intended primarily to burn with an aesthetically pleasing flame and with minimal heat being directed towards the room side of the appliance. This type of appliance is not intended to be used as a heat source and is not permitted to be equipped with or controlled by a thermostat. With technological advances in mechanical heating, cooling and ventilation systems, it is imperative that there is a consistency of use and operation, and that this equipment supports efficient, well-designed houses and occupancies. 594 Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 Energy Efficiency 9.36. 9.36.3.11. Solar Thermal Systems The NBC is silent on the use of renewable energy technologies; its requirements do not give credit where solar thermal equipment is used, and do not also create a barrier to its use. As the use of renewable energy technologies becomes more popular and installation or performance standards become available, these standards could be listed within the prescriptive path as an acceptable solution. The current NPC addresses solar thermal equipment and lists the appropriate standards for their installation. 9.36.4. Service Water Heating Systems NBC Subsection 9.36.4. addresses the selection and installation of service water heating systems and the efficient use of energy by service water heating systems. 9.36.4.1. Scope and Application This Article establishes the scope and limitations for the requirements pertaining to energy-efficient service water heating equipment and related components and systems. The requirements apply to service water heating systems that are typically installed in houses and small Part 9 buildings. Any building that employs service water heating systems or equipment that is not addressed within NBC

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: Subsection 9.36.3. must be designed and constructed in accordance with the energy efficiency requirements of the NECB. 9.36.4.2. Equipment Efficiency This Article provides a table with the proposed minimum efficiency values for various types of service water heating equipment that are typically installed in housing and small buildings, along with the appropriate performance requirements to which the equipment must conform. Gas-fired storage-type water heaters within the scope of CAN/CSA-P.3, “Testing method for measuring energy consumption and determining efficiencies of gas-fired and fuel oil-fired water heaters,” have their energy performance tested and expressed in terms of a uniform energy factor (UEF). Water heaters tested under previous versions of CAN/CSA-P.3 had their energy performance stated in terms of an energy factor (EF). As the industry transitions to using UEF, there may still be equipment on the market that is rated solely in terms of EF. UEF ratings are based on categories called “bins.” There are four different bins based on hot water usage. The UEF ratings are determined by assigning a water heater to a bin and evaluating the water heater's performance compared to other water heaters in the same bin. These evaluations are based on the first-hour rating. A water heater's UEF can only be compared to water heaters in the same bin. This

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: means that a water heater with a UEF of 0.95 from a high bin does not perform the same as a water heater with a UEF of 0.95 from a low bin. Within the same bin, a higher UEF means a water heater performs better compared to a water heater with a lower UEF. EF cannot be easily converted to UEF. NBC Table 9.36.4.2. provides the minimum requirement for UEF when the energy input and storage volume is known. UEF values should be provided by the water heater's manufacturer. Where equipment is rated in EF, compliance with the minimum UEF requirements for gas-fired storage-type water heaters can be achieved using NRCan's Minimum Energy Performance Standard (MEPS) formula, ≥0.675 −0.00039 Vr, where Vr, in l, is the rated nominal volume. Note that the MEPS formula represents equivalent energy performance, even though this formula may result in a different number than the actual or labeled number. A specific conversion equation must be used to make an acceptable comparison between EF and UEF values. Additional information is available in NRCan's Energy Efficiency Regulations: https://www.natural-resources.canada.ca/energy-efficiency/energy-efficiency-regulations/guide- canadas-energy-efficiency-regulations/gas-fired-storage-water-heaters-household/6901. Further information on the development of the ratings is provided in Guide 9.36.3.10., Equipment Efficiency. Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings 595

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 9.36. Energy Efficiency 9.36.4.3. Solar Domestic Hot Water Systems This Article addresses the installation of solar domestic hot water systems by referencing the NPC and requires that storage tanks be installed in a conditioned space. Further information on how solar domestic hot water systems are addressed by the NBC are provided in Guide 9.36.3.11., Solar Thermal Systems. 9.36.4.4. Piping This Article provides the requirements for the energy-efficient construction and design of piping for service water heating systems. Covering the first 2 m (6 ft. 7 in.) of outlet piping with insulation provides a simple method to reduce the heat loss through the pipes, which results in decreasing the amount of energy required to heat the water. The Article also includes minimum insulation requirements for recirculation lines. The requirements target periods of standby, where the water is not being used, and a substantial amount of heat loss from the pipes occurs directly adjacent to the tank. Insulating this portion of the pipes can reduce the heat loss at these locations. 9.36.4.5. Controls This Article requires that a hot water tank have

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: a temperature control device that allows the user to adjust the temperature of the hot water as desired, within the acceptable health and safety range. 9.36.4.6. Indoor Swimming Pool Equipment Controls This Article requires a means to automatically or manually switch off swimming pool pumps or heaters when their operation is not required. This saves the energy that would have been used to heat the water or run the pump to circulate the water. It may be necessary to operate the pump in order to filter the water enough to prevent the build-up of harmful bacteria and algae or to prevent the temperature of the water to drop too low. Manufacturers' requirements for pump use should be followed. 9.36.5. Energy Performance Compliance The performance compliance path follows the concept of establishing the energy performance of houses by comparing a proposed house to a reference house that is assumed to be built according to prescriptive Code requirements. This performance compliance approach is consistent with the objective-based Code approach of demonstrating a similar performance level regardless of the path used. The same concept is used for the performance path for buildings in the NECB. 9.36.5.1. Scope and Application This Article links the application of NBC Subsection 9.36.5. to the application of the prescriptive requirements described in NBC Subsection 9.36.1., and

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: limits the scope for the performance path option to houses, houses with secondary suites, and buildings that contain only dwelling units and common spaces where the common spaces occupy no more than 20% of the total floor area of the building. The reason for permitting only buildings of purely residential occupancy to be modeled is that the models currently on the market may not be able to deal with non-residential occupancies adequately. Likewise, it is not known how well energy modeling software for larger non-residential buildings performs when modeling small buildings. In addition, the loads and equipment used in dwelling units are well understood, and are less variable and more energy efficient. Therefore, they can be calculated with acceptable accuracy. Similarly, simple common spaces such as hallways and vestibules typically have no special equipment or highly variable loads, and their energy use can also be calculated with acceptable accuracy. Larger purely Part 9 residential buildings are known to use about 15% of the total floor area for hallways, staircases, vestibules and other small supporting common spaces. Placing a 20% limit on common spaces allows a margin to ensure smaller multi-unit residential buildings are not restricted from using the performance path. 596 Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 Energy Efficiency 9.36. 9.36.5.2. Definitions NBC Article 9.36.5.2. defines the terms “reference house” and “proposed house”, which are used throughout NBC Subsections 9.36.5. and 9.36.6. The reason for defining these terms is that they have no dictionary definitions and because the common meaning of these terms may be inappropriate to their use in NBC Subsection 9.36.5. The use of these terms without understanding the specific Code meaning could make the requirements, in which these terms appear, difficult to enforce, as well as make for inconsistent energy use calculations for houses and buildings. The term “reference house” refers to a modeled replica of the proposed house under consideration. The reference house includes all of the same energy sources and environmental characteristics as the proposed house, but it is made to comply with the requirements addressed in NBC Subsections 9.36.2. to 9.36.4. The term “proposed house” refers to a modeled replica of the actual house under consideration, with some elements that are addressed in NBC Subsections 9.36.2. to 9.36.4. modeled with values specific to the actual house. Elements that are not addressed in NBC Subsections 9.36.2. to 9.36.4., but may be necessary for calculating the annual energy consumption, will be assigned default values. The term “house” is used in this Article and throughout NBC Subsection 9.36.5. intentionally. It is meant to include residential buildings,

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: in contradiction to the term “building,” given the relation of the latter with the terms “building energy target,” “reference building,” and “proposed building,” which are used to refer to much larger buildings in the NECB. 9.36.5.3. Compliance This Article establishes the requirements to which the energy performance calculation procedure must conform. The performance path compares the simulated energy used by a proposed house to the energy used by a reference house that resembles the proposed house, but is modeled to meet the minimum prescriptive provisions of NBC Section 9.36. or NRCan's EnerGuide Rating System, with specific assumptions about other factors, including window area and building operation. If the simulation shows that the proposed house uses the same amount of energy or less than the reference house, it is deemed to comply with the NBC. Fundamentally, the performance path requires that two sets of calculation be performed: one for the proposed house, and the other for the reference house. The performance path provides greater flexibility in the design and specification of building components affecting energy use, and allows a designer to comply with the energy efficiency requirements of NBC Section 9.36. or the EnerGuide Rating System by using more energy-efficient building design features that exceed the prescriptive requirements of the NBC, such as the orientation of glazing to optimize solar gains. Additional reporting requirements are provided in NBC Division C, in order to standardize the compliance report requirements (i.e., features, component values and results). These administrative requirements only apply to demonstrating compliance with NBC Subsection 9.36.5. 9.36.5.4. Calculation Methods This Article

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: defines the portion of the calculation method that is common to both the reference and proposed houses. The Article also includes a list of calculation rules as well as default parameters and values for input into simulation tools. For example, it provides guidance on how computer models use climatic and location-specific data, how heat transfer through the building envelope needs to be calculated, and how the performance of HVAC and service water heating equipment must be modeled. While no particular software tools are prescribed, the development of the performance path was based on the default values and calculation procedures used in the NRCan HOT2000 software. NRCan may provide guidance for HOT2000 users on how to use HOT2000 for Code compliance using the performance path in NBC Part 9. The calculations of both the proposed house and the reference house must use the same tool, except where an exception for differences in building components or energy efficiency features are explicitly provided in NBC Subsection 9.36.5. The annual energy consumption for space conditioning, ventilation and service water heating systems is based on the primary equipment used, which is fixed for every day of the year by following the schedule provided for internal heat gain loads in NBC Table 9.36.5.4., and which is understood as the equipment that is required to meet the space-conditioning load of the house. Redundant or back-up equipment can, therefore, be excluded from the calculation, provided it is equipped with controls. Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings 597

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 9.36. Energy Efficiency Factors are provided to account for the heat gains produced by occupants, lighting and miscellaneous equipment. These are represented by a set of standard internal gains that are intended to compensate for the variability of occupant-driven behaviour from the calculation procedure. The scale factors applied to the load schedule are meant to account for the different occupant-driven loads observed in different types of residential buildings, and are based on the standard operating conditions used in the NRCan EnerGuide Rating System. 9.36.5.5. Climatic Data This Article describes the general requirements for the use of climatic data in the energy use simulation for both the reference and proposed houses. The NBC requires the use of climatic data measured at a time interval no greater than one hour for one year (8 760 hours) based on the average of at least 10 years of measured data collected at the weather station nearest to the region in which the proposed house is located. Climatic data sources include the Canadian Weather Year for Energy Calculations (CWEC) and the Canadian Weather Energy and Engineering Data Sets (CWEEDS). NBC Note A-9.36.5.5.(1) provides guidance for selecting the best representative data to use where climatic data for a

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: target location are not available. 9.36.5.6. Building Envelope Calculations This Article provides the requirements that pertain to the building envelope calculation methods that are common to both the reference and proposed houses. It specifies which building elements and related properties need to be included in the calculations. Credits may be applied to the calculation of the thermal mass and thermally active building assemblies. However, the ratio of transparent and opaque portions of windows and doors must be the same value for both the reference and proposed houses. The benefit of exterior shading can only be applied to the calculations of solar heat gain of windows and glazed doors. No shading benefits can be assumed for skylights or opaque building assemblies. 9.36.5.7. HVAC System Calculations This Article defines the requirements that pertain to the calculation methods that are common to both the reference and proposed houses for the heating, ventilating, and air conditioning, where installed, of houses. It specifies which systems and what relevant performance data need to be included in the calculations. A credit may be used in calculating the performance of ventilation, but the time period during which the ventilation equipment is assumed to be operating must be equal for both the reference and proposed houses. This requirement ensures that minimum ventilation is provided. The calculation method does not allow the internal temperature to exceed 25°C (77°F) during the heating season. This maximum temperature set-point (5.5°C (9.9°F) above 20°C

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: (68°F)) is based on an NRC research study(8) and requires that the calculation for both the proposed and reference houses treats internal temperature rise in a consistent manner. The calculation may, however, model excess heat as if it escaped through windows. Credit for reducing heat loss through piping is permitted, but the calculation needs to be applied consistently to both models for the reference and proposed houses. As well, a credit for better performing HRVs may be granted, provided the performance data is based on two data test points in accordance with the prescriptive requirements. 9.36.5.8. Service Water Heating System Calculations This Article defines the requirements that pertain to the service water heating equipment calculation methods common to both the reference and proposed houses. It specifies supply cold water temperatures depending on the climatic region in which the house is situated, and also sets the service water delivery temperature at 55°C (131°F). The energy model calculations must take into account daily service hot water usage for showering. A lower service water delivery temperature for showering of 41°C (105.8°F) at the shower head, with a reduced flow rate of 7.6 L/min, is now assumed, because of modern plumbing methods and showering habits. (8) S.A. Barakat and D.M. Saunder, The Utilization of Internal Heat Gains, Vol. 92(1A), pp. 103–115, National Research Council of Canada, Ottawa, 1986. 598 Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 Energy Efficiency 9.36. Some of the assumptions used in NBC Subsection 9.36.5. may not reflect the latest research in housing, and some discrepancies may exist compared with those used in NRCan's EnerGuide Rating System. 9.36.5.9. General Requirements for Modeling the Proposed House This Article requires that the calculations use the construction features described in drawings and specifications for the proposed house. NBC Note A-9.36.5.9.(1) contains a list of components that would typically be expected to be reflected in the calculations. 9.36.5.10. Modeling Building Envelope of Proposed House This Article provides the requirements that pertain to the energy model calculations in order to ensure that building envelope characteristics for the proposed house are consistent. Default values are provided for certain criteria to simplify the calculations, and keep them consistent with the calculations used for the reference house. With respect to foundation orientation, the construction of the actual house may be within 22.5° of the orientation used in the energy model calculations of the proposed house. This tolerance allows slight variations in site conditions that would otherwise prevent the actual house from being constructed and complying as shown in the permit drawings. An assumed airtightness value for the building may be used in the calculation procedure. A measured value, obtained

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: through a fan depressurization (blower door) test, can also be used. Default values for airtightness have been determined by using the average measured airtightness from houses across Canada. It was determined that if a house was built using the existing Code in that jurisdiction, the average airtightness observed by NRCan, calculated on the basis of thousands of sample houses, was 3.2 air changes per hour. Based on this value, it was projected that if the house was built according to the requirements of NBC Articles 9.36.2.9. and 9.36.2.10., a default value of 2.5 air changes per hour can be used for modeling. Where airtightness is measured, a design value is assigned for use in the calculation procedure until the actual airtightness has been measured. This value should be selected carefully to ensure that the level can be achieved. NBC Note A-9.36.7.3.(9) provides further information. Where measured airtightness is used in the calculation procedure, it shall be determined according to NBC Subsection 9.36.6. This requires testing in accordance with CAN/CGSB-149.10, “Determination of the airtightness of building envelopes by the fan depressurization method,” using a multi-point test, and the as-operated procedure in which some intentional openings in the building envelope are left unsealed during the test. The airtightness should be measured at a time in construction when the air barrier is complete, the mechanical equipment has been installed, and improvements could still be made should the house not reach the desired airtightness used in the energy model calculations.

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: 9.36.5.11. Modeling HVAC System of Proposed House This Article provides the requirements that pertain to the energy model calculations in order to ensure that the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning characteristics for the proposed house are consistent with the calculations. Default values are provided for certain criteria to simplify the calculations and ensure consistency with the values used for the reference house. The provisions in this Article deal with various types of heating/cooling equipment. The provisions only apply where such equipment is used. The principal ventilation rate is consistent with the requirements of NBC Section 9.32., and is based on the number of bedrooms in the proposed house. The part-load performance of the equipment in the proposed house is being kept the same as the reference house requirements for the same type of equipment. Using the actual manufacturer's data for part-load performance is also an option. Where an HRV is installed in the proposed house, the calculations only account for the recovery of sensible heat but not the latent heat (humidity). This still allows an energy efficiency credit for better HRV heat recovery performance, but does not give credit for potential additional savings from energy recovery ventilators (ERVs). For circulation fan flow rates and power requirements, several provisions are provided depending on the type of equipment that may be installed. The provisions provide options for determining rates for different scenarios. Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings 599

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 9.36. Energy Efficiency 9.36.5.12. Modeling Service Water Heating System of Proposed House This Article provides the requirements that pertain to the energy model calculations in order to ensure that the service water heating characteristics of the proposed house are consistent with the calculations. Default values are provided for certain criteria to simplify the calculations and ensure consistency with the criteria used for the reference house. Drain-water heat recovery systems may be used in the energy model calculations, with certain default values listed. The Article requires that the drain-water heat recovery system be modeled on the exact configuration in which it will be installed. In reality, there may be variations in the installation configuration that may undermine the intended benefit of the system in the energy model calculations. An assumed inlet temperature of 35°C (95°F) is specified to ensure realistic modeled energy savings. Provisions for multiple above-ground showers ensure that a meaningful proportion of shower heat is recovered, and that the benefit is not claimed without merit. 9.36.5.13. General Requirements for Modeling the Reference House This Article requires that the modeling assumptions for the reference house conform to the prescriptive requirements for the floor area, heated volume, and the number and types of rooms

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: of the proposed house. 9.36.5.14. Modeling Building Envelope of Reference House This Article requires that the energy model calculations be consistent with the building envelope characteristics of the reference house. Default values are provided for certain criteria and are based on common house construction according to the prescriptive requirements of the NBC. Airtightness values for attached houses that are tested without depressurizing the adjacent zones must be set at 3.0 air changes per hour. This is to acknowledge the fact that leakage through party walls, floors and ceilings cannot be separated from leakage to the exterior and does not significantly affect the overall energy performance of the house. Airtightness values for all other houses are set at 2.5 air changes per hour to recognize that a house is built according to the air barrier details described in NBC Article 9.36.2.10. The pressure exponent (PE) of a house can be determined using a multi-point depressurization test, and it relates to how airtightness varies with pressure difference. It reflects the type and size of holes through which the air is leaking. A value of 1.0 represents laminar flow through a long smooth-sided tube, while a value of 0.5 represents fully turbulent flow through a sharp-sided hole in a thin sheet. Theoretically, values lower than 0.5 or higher than 1.0 should not occur, but they are sometimes seen in tested houses because of the changing behaviour of the building envelope at pressure extremes. A

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: value of 0.67 is used as the default in the reference house if testing of the proposed houses does not result in a lower value; 0.67 is a typical value for the type of air leakage paths commonly found in houses. If two otherwise identical houses have the same ACH50, but one has a PE of 0.67 and the other has a value of 0.6, then at operational pressures up to 50 Pa the air leakage is likely to be higher in the house with a PE of 0.6. ACH50 is defined in NBC Article 9.36.6.2. Where there is no HRV, the default values to be used for the effective thermal resistance and overall thermal transmittance are those found in the tables of NBC Subsection 9.36.2. The calculations assume that the total area of the fenestration and the doors is evenly distributed around all sides of the house. There is no limit for the fenestration and door area to gross wall area ratio (FDWR) in the prescriptive path. However, in the performance path, the proposed house uses the actual FDWR according to its design and the reference house uses a value between 17% and 22% (see Figure 9.36.-17). Data collected from existing houses with one or two dwelling units in Canada show that the majority of housing has a FDWR in this range. 600 Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 Energy Efficiency 9.36. 17% 12% 12% 17% 22% 27% 22% 27% FDWR of the reference house credit penalty FDWR of the proposed house EG01391A Figure 9.36.-17 FDWR of the reference house depending on the FDWR of the proposed house For multi-unit residential buildings, the FDWR can be determined in more than one manner. If the FDWR is based on measuring the interior area of the exterior assemblies, the set FDWR for the reference house can be set in the same manner as for houses with one or two dwelling units. If the FDWR for the proposed house is measured using all the interior wall areas, including interior walls separating suites, the FDWR of the reference house follows that of the proposed house up to 40%. 9.36.5.15. Modeling HVAC System of Reference House This Article requires that the energy model calculations be consistent with the heating, ventilation, and air conditioning characteristics of the reference house. Default values are provided for certain criteria to simplify the calculations, and to ensure they are consistent with those used for the proposed house. The Article requires that

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: equipment be designed according to NBC Article 9.33.5.1., using CSA F280, “Determining the required capacity of residential space heating and cooling appliances.” It is important that the equipment not be oversized as this may have a negative effect on the energy model calculations. For the reference house, an HRV is not assumed, except where the presence of an indoor pool or spa requires dehumidification in NBC Sentence 9.36.3.8.(1) and an HRV is installed to perform this function. As a result, the installation of an HRV in the proposed house would generally constitute an additional benefit. For the equipment part-load performance requirements, the user can find pre-determined values in NBC Tables 9.36.5.15.-A to 9.36.5.15.-C, depending on the type of equipment. These factors are derived from the HOT2000 model tool, but values in other software tools for part-load performance are also acceptable. The performance of the HVAC equipment used in the reference house should match the type of equipment used in the proposed house. The base efficiency levels for the reference house equipment are as listed in NBC Table 9.36.3.10. Any increase in performance of the proposed house equipment constitutes an additional benefit. Where the table does not have the type of equipment used in the proposed house, the default for the reference house is set as a 95% gas warm-air furnace.

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: 9.36.5.16. Modeling Service Water Heating System of Reference House This Article requires that the energy model calculations be consistent with the service water heating characteristics of the reference house. Default values are provided for certain criteria to simplify the calculations and to ensure the criteria are consistent with those used for the proposed house. Wherever possible, the energy source of the equipment used in the reference house is the same as that used in the proposed house, and is set to the minimum performance efficiency found in NBC Table 9.36.4.2. NBC Table 9.36.5.16. provides the required capacities that are to be used where the proposed house has a tankless water heater. When the equipment used in the proposed house is not listed in NBC Table 9.36.4.2., the base default equipment of the reference house should be modeled as a gas-fired storage type water heater. 9.36.6. Airtightness of Building Envelope NBC Subsection 9.36.6. addresses the measuring of airtightness properties of buildings and dwelling units, and the use of test results to determine Airtightness Levels. Airtightness testing is not mandatory, but can be conducted to demonstrate Code compliance and, in some cases, may be less expensive for the builder than complying with the prescriptive airtightness requirements. Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings 601

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 9.36. Energy Efficiency 9.36.6.1. Scope and Application This Article establishes the scope and limitations of the airtightness requirements. Airtightness may be determined for use in energy modeling in compliance with NBC Subsection 9.36.5. or the tiered performance requirements of NBC Subsection 9.36.7. It may also be used to demonstrate an Airtightness Level, which can provide energy conservation points towards a prescriptive tier in NBC Article 9.36.8.8., or as an alternative to some prescriptive requirements in NBC Article 9.36.2.10. 9.36.6.2. Definitions NBC Article 9.36.6.2. defines a number of terms used throughout NBC Subsection 9.36.6. These are defined because their meaning is more specific than might be generally understood, or because they are acronyms that could otherwise be misinterpreted. The term “zone” can refer to the conditioned portion of a whole building or a unit within the building, such as an attached house, condominium or row house. It may sometimes be necessary for a large house or building to be tested as multiple zones, because test equipment cannot otherwise achieve a uniform enough pressure within the zone. Testing of a zone will provide the air leakage rate of the area being tested. It is important to understand that the result of a test cannot, in most cases, be extrapolated to other areas of the house, as these areas will have different constructions. If testing is done on all zones, the values may be

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: combined to provide an overall result, provided that the tests are guarded or that the air leakage between zones is taken into consideration. The zone should have a suitably large opening, usually a door or window, to allow the test equipment to be installed. The term “attached zone” is intended to cover houses (or zones within a house) that touch an adjacent zone through shared walls, floors, ceilings, or junctions, and through which conditioned air might flow. This includes semi-detached houses, row houses, houses constructed that touch an existing building, and multi-unit residential buildings. In the latter case, adjacent zones include those connected by a single corner or edge, as well as those connected by a whole face (see Figure 9.36.-18). EG02885A Unit 1 is considered an attached zone with Units 2, 5 and 6. Dwelling Unit 1 Zone 1 Unit 10 Unit 6 Unit 2 Unit 9 Unit 5 Unit 1 Dwelling Unit 2 Zone 2 shared wall Figure 9.36.-18 Example of attached zones The term “ACH50” refers to the number of times a volume of air equalling the volume of the tested zone would be replaced if a pressure difference of 50 Pascals (Pa) was maintained for one hour. Small houses often perform worse on this metric when compared to equivalent large houses, because: • leakage through mechanical equipment and ducts does not reduce proportionally with house volume, and • air leakage is often concentrated around junctions, edges and corners, which tends to make a larger contribution for smaller zones. 602 Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 Energy Efficiency 9.36. The term “NLA10” refers to the normalized air leakage area. It is the equivalent area of a sharp-edged hole per unit area of envelope, which would have the same air leakage as the tested zone at a pressure difference of 10 Pa. The term “NLR50” refers to the normalized air leakage rate, which is the volume of air leaving a given area of the building envelope in the unit time at a pressure difference of 50 Pa. The results for small houses will often be better using this metric as opposed to ACH50, as small houses have a larger surface area–to-volume ratio. 9.36.6.3. Determination of Airtightness Airtightness testing completed for the requirements of NBC Section 9.36. must comply with CAN/CGSB-149.10, “Determination of the airtightness of building envelopes by the fan depressurization method,” and must use the “as-operated” conditions set out in that standard. The test may be guarded or unguarded. The standard explains these terms in more detail, but in simple terms: • “As-operated” means that air leakage through mechanical equipment and fans is included in the result. The equipment can be switched off and dampers closed, if present, but no sealing of these elements is permitted. This condition was selected for consistency, and to better reflect air leakage in the occupied dwelling. • A guarded test is one where all zones that are adjacent to the tested zone are also depressurized to the test pressure, in order to eliminate the air leakage between conditioned spaces. This test is

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: used when determining the air leakage through only part of a building or a single attached zone. An example of when this method would be used is when the goal is to determine the air leakage of exterior walls only, and not the air leakage to adjacent rooms, floors or zones. A guarded test requires that pressurization devices be set up in the adjacent zones, so the measured air leakage is only to the exterior or to unconditioned spaces. This will provide a value for that interface only, and will not account for air leakage between the attached units or zones. • An unguarded test is one where, if there are adjacent zones, only the tested zone is depressurized. Air leakage to or from adjacent zones will contribute to the result. This test method is simpler when compared to the guarded method, and can be conducted in attached zones as each dwelling is completed, with minimal disturbance to adjacent dwellings. In attached zones, this method measures the air leakage from a larger surface area than a guarded test. Therefore, an allowance is made to adjust the reference house in NBC Sentence 9.36.5.14.(2), and an alternative table for Airtightness Levels is provided in NBC Sentence 9.36.6.4.(4). The unguarded test result is accurate for that zone; however, adding the air leakage of multiple zones together is not expected to predict the total air leakage of a building. Airtightness testing for use in energy modeling (for NBC Subsection 9.36.5. or 9.36.7.) must use a multi-point test, and is required to report the ACH50 value, along with the pressure exponent and the equivalent leakage area. Determination of these values requires a multi-point test, in order to achieve sufficient accuracy for modeling purposes. Airtightness testing

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: to demonstrate an Airtightness Level can use a single-, two- or multi-point test, as desired, and need only report one of the ACH50, NLA10 or NLR50 values. Note, however, that a single-point test is not permitted to be used to determine NLA10 as it would not be sufficiently accurate. Single- and two-point tests are quicker to perform than multi-point tests and provide enough information for the allocation of points. See NBC Note A-9.36.6.4.(2) for more information. 9.36.6.4. Determination of Airtightness Level To find energy conservation points for an Airtightness Level as set out by NBC Article 9.36.8.8., all zones in the building should be tested. Airtightness Levels can be demonstrated through any one of the airtightness metric results (ACH50, NLA10 or NLR50) for the tested zones. The NBC allows points to be assessed using any or all of the three metrics, and considers compliance through a single metric to be sufficient. NBC Table 9.36.6.4.-A describes the threshold values for each level in detached houses and in attached zones using a guarded test. NBC Table 9.36.6.4.-B should be used for buildings with attached zones, using an unguarded test on each zone. This table assumes a different equivalence between ACH50 and the other two parameters, which better reflects houses tested this way. The actual conversion between metrics depends on the geometry of the zone. If a building contains more than one zone, a combination of more than one airtightness metric is permitted when determining the worst-case Airtightness Level. If more than one airtightness metric is calculated for a tested zone, the best result would be determined by the highest-level airtightness metric for each zone Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings 603

Tiered Energy Performance Compliance: Performance Path Energy performance tiers were developed as part of the goal to create requirements for Part 9 residential buildings that lead to high performance, low energy use buildings. NBC Subsection 9.36.7. addresses the performance simulation approach to meeting the energy performance tiers. Each tier corresponds to either the difference between the annual energy consumption of the proposed house and the house energy target, expressed as a percentage (percent improvement metric); or the result of dividing the annual energy consumption by the house energy target of the reference house, expressed as a percentage (house energy target metric). Provincial building codes may choose to adopt all performance tiers, or make them optional. Check your applicable building code for clarification. The performance compliance path establishes the energy performance of houses by comparing a proposed house to a reference house that is assumed to be built according to prescriptive Code requirements. This performance compliance approach is consistent with the objective-based Code approach of demonstrating a similar performance level regardless of the path used. See Guide Appendix C for a suggested tiered energy performance compliance performance path checklist. 604 Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 Energy Efficiency 9.36. 9.36.7.1. Scope and Application This Article limits the scope for the performance path option to buildings and to houses with secondary suites. To assess an attached house individually, the heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) and the service water heating systems must only serve the house, its secondary suite or both. The house must not have common spaces intended for occupancy (such as corridors and staircases) with other dwelling units and houses, unless it is for a secondary suite. Houses not meeting these requirements must be assessed as part of the larger building containing them. 9.36.7.2. Compliance Compliance with the tiered energy requirements is determined by comparing the difference in performance of the proposed house to the reference house using several metrics. The proposed house must achieve a greater heat loss reduction than the reference house. In addition, the proposed house must meet either the “percent improvement” target or the “percent house energy” target set out in NBC Table 9.36.7.2. Total Volume of Conditioned Space within the Building or House The total volume of conditioned space within the building or house metric is used

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: to determine which target energy performance a proposed house should comply with. There are two energy performance targets that can be achieved by using percent heat loss reduction and either the percent improvement target or the percent energy target. The target energy performance for buildings or houses also depends on whether the total volume is less than or equal to 300 m3 (10 594 ft.3), and where the total volume is greater than 300 m3 (10 594 ft.3). Where the volume of conditioned space has not been determined, a volume greater than 300 m3 (10 594 ft.3) is assumed. This is shown in NBC Table 9.36.7.2. The total volume of conditioned space within the building or the house refers to the volume measured at the interior surfaces of exterior walls, ceilings and floors of a house (see Figure 9.36.-19). EG02886A The volume of internal floors and walls is included when calculating the representative volume. Figure 9.36.-19 Volume of conditioned space within the building or house 9.36.7.3. Energy Performance Improvement Compliance Calculations There are several metrics that need to be understood and calculated in order to demonstrate compliance using the checklist for the tiered energy performance compliance: performance path. The calculations to determine these metrics are described below. Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings 605

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 9.36. Energy Efficiency To calculate the percent heat loss reduction, work out the difference between the annual gross space heat loss for the proposed house and the annual gross space heat loss for the reference house, divide by the annual gross space heat loss for the reference house, and multiply the answer by 100. To calculate the annual gross space heat loss required for the percent heat loss reduction target, add together the cumulative heat loss due to conduction in the building envelope, the infiltration, the exfiltration, and the mechanical ventilation. The HOT2000 modeling software automatically generates the annual gross space heat loss. The percent improvement and percent house energy target metrics are two different ways of expressing the same energy performance of the proposed house. These metrics are relative to the reference house. For example, if the proposed house achieves a 10% improvement when compared to the reference house, then it will use 90% of the energy that the reference house uses. To calculate the percent improvement, work out the difference between the

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: annual energy consumption of the proposed house and the house energy target of the reference house, divide by the house energy target of the reference house, and multiply the answer by 100. To calculate the percent house energy target, divide the annual energy consumption of the proposed house by the house energy target of the reference house, and multiply the answer by 100. Peak Cooling Load The peak cooling load refers to the highest hourly averaged rate of heat removed from a conditioned space to maintain a comfortable temperature in a house or building over the course of a year. The peak cooling load does not reflect the rate of energy consumed by any cooling equipment. Some modeling software, including HOT2000, generates a “design cooling load,” which is an acceptable alternative to peak cooling load according to NBC Note A-9.36.7.3.(4). To comply with NBC Subsection 9.36.7., the peak cooling load for the proposed house cannot be greater than the peak cooling load for the reference house. Where a proposed house is not expected to meet the peak cooling requirement, some adjustments to the design may help; for example: reducing the solar heat gain coefficient of the fenestration used, reducing the area of the glazing, or adjusting the orientation of fenestration. Adding air

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: conditioning will not help meet the requirement. NBC Note A-9.36.7.3.(4) provides guidance for any additional modeling required. Differences in Modeling from Subsection 9.36.5. It is important to note that there are some additional requirements when modeling the proposed house for compliance with NBC Subsection 9.36.6. when compared to NBC Subsection 9.36.5. These additional requirements are specified in NBC Article 9.36.6.3., and described below. When seeking to attain energy performance Tier 2 or higher, if space heating in the proposed house is provided by a heat pump, then the reference house must be modeled using the same heating system as the secondary or back-up system of the proposed house. Alternatively, if the proposed house has no back-up system specified, the reference house can be modeled using electric resistance heating. This requirement does not apply for energy performance Tier 1, because there is no heat loss reduction target to ensure the envelope has adequate performance as well. The percent heat loss reduction target is based on the annual gross space heat loss. The annual gross space heat loss is a good representation of heat loss through a building envelope as it accounts for heat loss due to 606 Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: © His Majesty the King in Right of Canada, as represented by the National Research Council of Canada, 2025 © Sa Majesté le Roi du chef du Canada, représenté par le Conseil national de recherches du Canada, 2025 Energy Efficiency 9.36. conduction and air leakage, while excluding solar and internal gains. The annual gross space heat loss is also easily extracted from building simulation models. NBC Article 9.36.6.3. also provides guidance for modeling airtightness. Testing for airtightness is voluntary and there are no targets prescribed for builders or designers who choose to conduct an airtightness test. Airtightness is a significant factor in determining energy efficiency performance. Regardless of whether an airtightness test is conducted or not, the airtightness value must be specified when modeling the proposed house. If no airtightness test is conducted, the proposed house must be modeled using the default airtightness value of 3.2 air changes per hour at a pressure difference of 50 Pa and a pressure exponent of 0.67. When conducting an airtightness test, if applicable, a design airtightness value is assigned for use in the calculation procedure until the actual airtightness has been measured. This value should be selected carefully to ensure that the level can be achieved. Where measured airtightness is used in the calculation procedure, it will be determined according to NBC Subsection 9.36.6. After the airtightness test has been conducted, the proposed house can be modeled using the measured airtightness value, assuming that the measured airtightness value meets the chosen

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: design airtightness value or is lower than 2.5 air changes per hour. If the measured airtightness value does not meet the design airtightness value and is greater than 2.5 air changes per hour, and complies with the prescriptive measures in NBC Clause 9.36.5.10.(9)(b), then the airtightness value of 2.5 air changes per hour may be used. Otherwise, the default value of 3.2 air changes per hour must be used. NBC Note A-9.36.7.3.(9) clarifies how to determine the correct airtightness value to use. 9.36.8. Tiered Energy Performance Compliance: Prescriptive Path In the development of requirements for Part 9 buildings of residential occupancy that will lead to high performance, low energy use buildings, there has been interest in having a flexible prescriptive approach that does not require simulation. NBC Subsection 9.36.8. addresses the prescriptive approach to meeting energy performance tiers. Provincial building codes may choose to adopt all prescriptive tiers, or make them optional. Consult your applicable building code for clarification. The prescriptive tier path introduces a points-based approach to meeting energy performance improvement tiers. Points are assessed for the whole building, not for dwellings within the building; for example, a single score would apply to an entire multi-unit residential building, a set of row houses or a pair of semi-detached houses. The building must meet all prescriptive requirements described in NBC Subsections 9.36.2. to 9.36.4., except where points are claimed for exceeding these requirements. If a building falls in between the points criteria, interpolation and extrapolation of points and

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: tiers are not permitted. See Guide Appendix C for a suggested checklist for the tiered energy performance compliance: prescriptive path. In developing this section, the energy use of 240 archetypical Canadian houses was assessed using a minimum specification from the NBC, with the addition of each measure individually. The typical percentage saving for each climate zone was used to set the points available. It is expected that, on average, buildings that implement measures that achieve ten points, for example, would then use ten percent less energy than when constructed according to the requirements of NBC Subsections 9.36.2. to 9.36.4. For this reason, the number of points for some measures does not increase consistently with the climate zone, as the Code minimum is also increasing. 9.36.8.5. Energy Conservation Measures for Above-Ground Opaque Building Assemblies Points for above-ground opaque building assemblies may be based on the allowable effective thermal resistance for the assembly and the heating degree-days associated with the building location, as shown in NBC Table 9.36.8.5. Table 9.36.-C below provides examples of common building assemblies that reach the minimum effective thermal resistance values shown in NBC Table 9.36.8.5. NBC Note A-9.36.2.6.(1) contains additional assembly configurations that may be helpful. The effective thermal resistances of assemblies may vary depending on cladding materials. The CWC's free online Effective R Calculator provides additional wall assembly examples. You can access this calculator at www.cwc.ca/en/design-tools/effective-r-calculator/. Energy Conservation Measures for Fenestration and Doors The U-value or Energy Rating (ER) of fenestration and doors may be used to claim points where they exceed the minimum requirements set out in NBC Article 9.36.2.7. Skylights and glass block assemblies are not assessed in this calculation. Points for fenestration and doors may be awarded based on the maximum allowable fenestration or U-value of the door in the building, or by using a trade-off calculation. Individual doors or fenestrations may demonstrate compliance through ER, provided the total area of openings in the building face is less than 17% of the wall area of the face. This is similar to the fenestration and door area to gross wall ratio (FDWR) calculation, but broken down by orientation. Fenestration or doors complying through ER should be excluded from the U-value trade-off calculation. This facilitates compliance with elements such as patio doors, which might otherwise not be able to meet the target U-value. See Figure 9.36.-20 for an example of how to calculate the percent fenestration area. 608 Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings

title: Illustrated Users Guide NBC2020 Part9
text: (SHGC) into a building, the thermal heat flow out of a building (U-value), and the air leakage heat flow out of a building. The ER is only applicable for small residential buildings. The higher the ER, the more energy efficient the product is in a cold climate, because the increased solar heat gain reduces the heating load of the building. The intent of the ER is to indicate the relative energy performance of fenestration system products over the heating season. Energy Efficiency For buildings with two or more dwellings, it is permissible to test the whole building (if feasible) or to test each dwelling unit individually, as well as the common space, and take the test result with the highest air leakage level when determining the energy conservation points. As an example, a 4-unit row house is under construction in Barrhaven, a suburb of Ottawa, Ontario (4500 HDD, climate zone 6). The builder would like to comply with prescriptive energy performance Tier 2 of the NBC, which represents a total of 10 points. The above-grade walls of the row house have an effective wall RSI value of 3.85. This means that the building has already achieved 6.9 energy conservation points in climate zone 6 (See NBC Table 9.36.8.5.). The remainder of the points will be met through the building airtightness. To help maximize the potential points able to be achieved, the airtightness will be tested using all three metrics (ACH, NLA and NLR). Unguarded airtightness testing will be used, as the units in the row house will be occupied in stages. The test results are provided in Table 9.36.-D: Table 9.36.-D Test Results for an Example 4-unit Row House in Climate Zone 6 Left End House Left Middle House Right Middle House Right End House ACH 1.49 2.01 1.95 1.51 NLA 0.97 1.29 1.24 0.95 NLR 0.57 0.75 0.79 0.60 Because the airtightness testing is unguarded in attached zones, the tier achieved by each row house unit must be determined using NBC Table 9.36.6.4.-B. Then, the best

According to NBC Table 9.36.8.8., AL-3B achieves 3.5 energy conservation points for climate zone 6. In this case, the builder will be able to achieve a total of 10.4 points (3.5 plus 6.9 for the above-grade walls). This will meet the prescriptive performance Tier 2 requirements. 9.36.8.9. Energy Conservation Measures for HVAC Systems Use of unconventional space heating systems not listed in NBC Subsection 9.36.3. is not compatible with this compliance path and will require assessment under the NECB. In all cases, a heat recovery ventilator (HRV) is required as a prerequisite for any tier in this path. Note that an energy recovery ventilator (ERV) is a subset of an HRV, and is an acceptable means of complying with this requirement. Using ventilation equipment that is more efficient than the minimum sensible recovery efficiency (SRE) percentage described in NBC Article 9.36.3.9. can earn points, as set out in NBC Table 9.36.8.9. 610 Illustrated User's Guide – NBC 2020: Part 9 of Division B, Housing and Small Buildings

Energy Conservation Measures for Service Water Heating Equipment Use of unconventional service water heating equipment that is not listed in NBC Subsection 9.36.4. is not compatible with this compliance path and would require assessment under the NECB. However, systems that meet the requirements of NBC Table 9.36.8.10. are eligible for points. Combined space- and water-heating systems can earn points in this category, as described in Note (2) of NBC Table 9.36.8.10. The water heating aspect of these systems should have an EF or UEF rating, in addition to the overall thermal performance factor (TPF), which can be used to verify compliance. 9.36.8.11. Energy Conservation Points for Building Volume Points are available for buildings with lesser volume of conditioned space, as they may use less energy than those having larger conditioned space. If the building is eligible for points, the volume of the building and all dwelling units, as applicable, can be measured at the interior surface of the thermal envelope. If the basement is conditioned, it should be included in this calculation. Figure 9.36.-21 illustrates how building volume is calculated for different types of dwellings. There are two ways to gain energy conservation points. In the first option, each dwelling unit within a building must be less than 230 m3 (8 122 ft.3), in which case 10 credits can be awarded, regardless of the total volume of the building. The second option sets an upper limit for total building volume of 390 m3 (13 772 ft.3) for points to be awarded, which most likely will apply to detached houses. NBC Sentence 9.36.8.11.(2) gives increasing points for 10 m3 (353 ft.3) bands below this volume. Interpolation is not permitted. Some are issued under the authority of the code or the Safety Codes Act as provincewide variances or interpretations. Others are information bulletins that provide general advice on related matters. Variances Variance under the Safety Codes Act . All variances are available through Open Government records. title: Building advisories, bulletins and variances
text: Building advisories, bulletins and variances Information Information | Stage 4 water restrictions are in effect starting Nov. 4. Find out how construction activities may be impacted and how to prepare. View construction guidance Building advisories, bulletins and variances These documents offer clarification on the application of the National Building Code – Alberta Edition, Canadian Electrical Code, National Plumbing Code and the Natural Gas and Propane Installation Code, as well as The City’s Land Use Bylaw. A bulletin is a regulation under a code. An advisory is an interpretation of a code or municipal regulation. A variance is written permission to modify the application of the code, provided that an equivalent or greater level of safety is provided. All advisories, bulletins and variances posted, regardless of year of development and code cycle under which they were originally published, are valid. Note, these documents are subject to removal at any time. Advisories have no legal status and cannot be used as an official interpretation of the various bylaws, codes, and regulations currently in effect. The City of Calgary accepts no responsibility to persons relying solely on this information. New Building Code resources Please follow the links for more information regarding upcoming changes to The National Building Code - 2023 Alberta Edition, National Fire Code - 2023 Alberta Edition and the National Energy Code of Canada for Buildings 2020 that will come into force on May 1, 2024. title: CCMC registry of product assessments
text: CCMC registry of product assessments - National Research Council Canada CCMC registry of product assessments This registry contains the most up-to-date version of our product assessments. Assessments are considered active as long as they are published here. Assessments that have been withdrawn are no longer in the registry but are available upon request by contacting the CCMC at ccmc@nrc-cnrc.gc.ca or 613-993-6189 . Users should consult the registry to verify an assessment’s publication status and version (last modified date) prior to its use. JSON Application Programming Interface (API) alternative format This index page is available for access by digital systems through the CCMC Registry of Product Assessments JSON Application Programming Interface (API) . An API is an interface that allows for communication between different software systems. The registry uses JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) to structure the information in the assessments according to the specifications in the table below. Each API record represents one CCMC product assessment. API specificatons Field Value Description Id Number The unique identifier of the assessment. ccmcno String The unique seven-character CCMC number assigned to the assessment that can be found on the product and in product literature (e.g., "03240-L"). organization_eng String The name of the assessment holder organization in English. organization_fre String or null The name of the assessment holder organization in French (if different from English). website_eng String or null The website of the assessment holder organization in English. website_fre String or null The website of the assessment holder organization in French (if different from English). organization_id Number The unique identifier of the assessment holder organization. status_eng String "Active" The status of the assessment holder in English. (Currently only "Active" assessments are included in the registry; this may change in the future.) status_fre String "En vigeur" The status of the assessment holder

Roof Truss Engineering Requirements for New Construction Building Permits Effective March 1, 2026 , applicants must provide roof truss assemblies authenticated by an Alberta-licensed engineering professional with the building permit application. This includes all Part 9 Buildings, such as single-family or semi-detached homes and 3- and 4-unit row houses. For more information, review the Policy Bulletin B23-03 Roof Truss Engineering Requirements . Applications can be submitted online or mailed to the Edmonton Service Centre . This page lists the minimum submission requirements. Applications missing any required plans, documents and details will not be accepted. The current land use regulation is Zoning Bylaw 20001 Alberta's building code, effective 01 May 2024, is the National Building Code-2023 Alberta Edition Auto-Review in Developing Areas The City uses an Auto-Review process for Development Permit applications for Single Detached and Semi-detached houses in developing areas that are zoned Small-Scale Flex Residential Zone (RSF). How Does it Work? When applying for eligible projects online , the interactive application process will enable you to verify a project complies with applicable zoning regulations. Projects that meet the Auto-Review criteria may obtain a Development Permit in as little as 1 day, greatly reducing timelines,

title: Application Requirements for House Permits
text: especially during peak construction season. Resources and Education How-to Guide Applicant Responsibilities The City uses Auto-Review to assist in the Development Permit application approval process. Applicants complete the application form and confirm the information they have submitted is accurate and complete. The information entered into the application is verified for compliance with the Zoning Bylaw and is used as the basis for the Development Permit decision. Drawings and plans are still required to be provided with the Development Permit application. The City will audit applications selected at random to confirm the accuracy of the information submitted and compliance with all applicable regulations. Accurate and complete information is essential. A Development Permit issued on the basis of incorrect information contained in the application is invalid. A Development Permit may be cancelled if the application for the Development Permit contained a material misrepresentation, if the Development Permit was issued as a result of a material error and/or if material facts were not disclosed at any time during the application process for the Development Permit. If the City becomes aware of incorrect, inaccurate or misleading information provided in the application by the applicant, either knowingly or unknowingly, any issued Development Permit may be deemed invalid from the date of issuance and the City will not be liable for any claims, damages or costs associated with the Development Permit or application. Project Eligibility Most new single and semi-detached house applications in lots zoned small-scale flex residential (RSF) in developing neighbourhoods are eligible for Auto-Review. To qualify, projects must be on registered lots and meet all requirements of the Zoning Bylaw. Ineligible projects include multi-unit housing, lots that are within the top of bank and reduced setback developments . For a complete list of eligible and

title: Application Requirements for House Permits
text: ineligible projects, see the How-to Guide . Applications that do not meet the required criteria will be redirected to a Development Planner for a review and decision. These applications will take more time for a decision to be rendered and will be processed in the order received. After You Apply Following submission of the Development Permit application, here is what to expect: Development Permit is issued - All aspects entered through Auto-Review meet eligibility criteria. A Development Permit is provided within a few minutes by email notification to the applicant and includes a House Design report that lists the details provided in the application. Or Development Permit Application is audited - All aspects entered through Auto-Review meet the eligibility criteria but through a random audit process, the application is selected for an audit. A few minutes after submission of the application, you will see the application proceed to “In Development Review” for review by a Development Planner. Following a successful audit, the Development Permit will be issued. If corrections are made to your application submission, City staff will notify you and issue the permit with a copy of the House Design report that includes the revised details. If issues are found, a Development Planner will contact you. Or Review by a Development Planner - The entered information does not meet Auto-Review criteria, or the application does not comply with the Zoning Bylaw, and/or requires a variance . The application will be sent to a Development Planner for a review and decision. As part of the Building Permit processing, further clarification may be sought if omissions are found with the Development Permit application. Low-Impact Development (LID) is a type of stormwater management facility that incorporates plants, engineered soils and natural processes to capture stormwater runoff close to its source. Eligibility Applicants have the option to include LID as part of a new development. Corner infill sites of 3 or 4 units that propose LID and follow the Low-Impact Development Guidelines for Corner Lot Infill Developments are eligible for streamlined EPCOR and City of Edmonton approvals of the facility. The guidelines contain details about standardized designs, plant species recommendations, drawing and submission requirements, construction and maintenance considerations, and soil specifications. If you have questions about LID, contact LIDoutreach@epcor.com . As part of a Development Permit application that contains an LID facility, the submission package must include a site mechanical plan, stormwater management calculations, a Lot Grading Plan, and Landscaping Plan. title: Single Stair
text: Single Stair Alternative Solutions: CMHC Housing Supply Challenge ︎ Single Stair Alternative Solutions Prototypes Pilot Projects Haeccity AIR studio KHA 5468796 Invizij SvN mcCallumSather LGA Office Ou Lateral Office Report on Single Exit Stair (SES) Building Design Technical Report on Mechanical Smoke Control Systems LCA Study of Exit Stairs LCA Study of Prototypes FAQ About CMHC Housing Supply Challenge Round 4: Building for the Future This website is a knowledge mobilization deliverable published in January 2025 and is provided for information purposes only. Single Stair Alternative Solutions Design Innovation for Middle Housing Prescriptive building codes across Canada require two means of egress for any multi-unit residential building exceeding two storeys. However, a review of codes across other jurisdictions shows that multiplexes and small apartment buildings can be safely constructed with a single exit stair. This approach supports gentle density, maximizing land use on small sites while improving sustainability, accessibility and design flexibility. Single exit stair (SES) building design adds enough floor area for at least another bedroom on each storey of a building and improves the feasibility of infill housing on small properties. The solution also allows for apartment layouts with more natural light and fresh air, as well as making it easier to provide an elevator to make three-storey buildings fully accessible. For inquiries: singlestair@lga-ap.com April 2025 - This research project was awarded The RAIC Research & Innovation in Architecture Award by the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada and was featured in Canadian Architect magazine. Jury Comments: “This meticulous study of single exit stair building code reform presents a transformative approach to addressing Canada's housing challenges. Through richly documented

title: Energy efficiency Tier 1 of section 9.36.
text: Building STANDATA | Alberta.ca ©2024 Government of Alberta | Published: April 2024 | Municipal Affairs STANDATA bulletin 23-BCB-001 Building Energy efficiency Tier 1 of section 9.36. Date Issued: April 2024 Page 1 of 2 Purpose To provide information regarding the changes to the adopted energy efficiency Tier 1 of Section 9.36. of the National Building Code - 2023 Alberta Edition (NBC(AE)). Discussion In Alberta, Tier 1 is the minimum province-wide standard for building energy efficiency for housing and small buildings as identified in Section 9.36. of the NBC(AE). The Tier 1 reference is Article 9.36.1.3. for compliance and application. Article 9.36.7.3. is identified as an option where an owner voluntarily builds to a tier higher than Tier 1. The following has been adopted/incorporated into the NBC(AE): 1. The airtightness used in the energy code calculations for the proposed house would comply with Clause 9.36.5.10.(9)(a) or 9.36.5.10.(9)(b). 2. The use of a single air change per hour(ACH) of 2.5 provides consistency in the application of the code requirements, instead of a two-level system for ACH for houses. The following is not applicable for Tier 1 of the NBC(AE): 1. Peak cooling load requirements of 9.36.7. 2. This method would be used when calculating energy performance improvement compliance for the higher tiers and applying the same equipment and loads from Tier 1 to higher tiers. For the NBC(AE), Subsections 9.36.2 to 9.36.4. Prescriptive Path and 9.36.5 Performance Path are deemed as the minimum for compliance with Alberta’s Tier 1. Sentence 9.36.1.3.(2) of Alberta’s code edition is important to note, as the higher tiers referenced in accordance with Subsection 9.36.7. or 9.36.8. are optional. The Appendix note for Sentence 9.36.1.3.(2) explains that while the higher levels of tier code are presented, they are not enforceable under the Safety Codes Act. Alberta specific changes
